resources.string: Notification access

The island exists to show your notifications, so it has to be allowed to see them. This is the one broad permission the app needs. What it reads is held in memory for as long as the island shows it, and never written to disk.
Show a notification on the island: the icon the app put on it, its title, text and action buttons
Let you reply inline, or trigger an action, and pass that straight back to the app that posted it
Dismiss the real notification when you swipe the island away
Detect an ongoing or incoming call, and the system countdown behind a timer notification

Read what is playing for the music tile — track, artist, album art and playback state — and send your previous, play, pause and next taps back to the player. Android ties this to the same grant, so it is this permission that makes the music tile work
Vibration permission
Used to produce vibrations and haptic feedback through the app and the cutout
Vibrate when going through the app
Providing haptic feedback when clicking on the cutout
Accessibility service

Android only lets an accessibility service draw a window that survives above other apps and the lockscreen. That window is the island, so the service is mostly used as a drawing surface. It reads no screen content: the only thing it looks at is the package name of the foreground app. Anything read is drawn on the island and dropped — never written to disk, never logged, and with no internet permission it cannot leave the device.
Draw the island over the camera cutout, above whatever app is in the foreground
Keep it there across app switches, and tear it down while the device is locked if you asked for that
Receive your taps and swipes on the island itself
Read the name of the app in the foreground — its package name only, no screen content — so the music tile can hide itself while the app playing the music is open
Ignore battery optimisation

Optional. Without it, aggressive power management can kill the overlay in the background, and the island stops appearing until you reopen the app. There is no sync, no polling and no scheduled job behind it — the app idles until something reaches the island.
Ask the system, once, to leave the overlay service running
Post notifications
Optional, and only asked for on Android 13 and later, the first time you tap one of the test buttons on the Permissions screen. The app posts nothing you did not ask for.
Post the sample notification, call and reply used to preview the island without waiting for a real one
Audio settings

Used by two buttons on the expanded phone tile. No dialer offers mute or speakerphone as a notification action, so the tile drives the audio route itself. It changes nothing on its own, and records no audio — this permission cannot.
Mute and unmute the microphone during a call, from the expanded phone tile
Put a call on speakerphone and take it off again
Phone state

Optional, and asked for only on the Permissions screen. It reports whether a call is ringing, connected or over — nothing else. It gives no phone number, no caller identity and no call log; the caller shown on the island comes from the dialer\'s own notification, as it always has. Without it the phone tile still closes when a call ends, just from the notification panel, which can take a few seconds.
Close the phone tile the moment a call ends, instead of waiting to notice the dialer\'s notification is gone
Shizuku access

Optional, and only used by three features that Android reserves for the shell user. Shizuku is a separate app you install and start yourself; it holds those shell privileges and lends them to apps you approve, one at a time, in its own interface. Without it those features are simply unavailable — everything else works as normal. The app talks to Shizuku only while you have one of them switched on.
Hide the system status bar\'s notification icons, alerts and clock, so the island is the only thing reporting notifications. This needs STATUS_BAR, which an ordinary app cannot hold

Read which apps are using the microphone, camera or location right now, so the island can draw the privacy dots. This needs GET_APP_OPS_STATS, which an ordinary app cannot hold. The dot says only that something is in use, never which app, and the check runs only while the feature is switched on
Read the list of devices connected to your hotspot (MAC address and device name), only while the hotspot is on and the option is enabled
Network state

Read-only, granted automatically, and never prompted for. It reports whether you are connected and the name of the network you are on — it grants no internet access, and cannot see networks you are not connected to.
Show the Wi-Fi connect and disconnect event on the island, with the network name
Wi-Fi state

Read-only, granted automatically, and never prompted for. Since Android 12L the system only tells apps holding this permission when the hotspot turns on or off; without it the hotspot event would never fire. It cannot turn Wi-Fi or the hotspot on, cannot see who is connected to it, and grants no internet access. It covers only the on/off event, not the list of connected devices.
Show the hotspot enabled and disabled event on the island
App list visibility

Not a permission you grant, but a manifest entry, so it is listed here too. On Android 11 and later an app sees no other app unless it declares what it needs to see. This one asks for apps that have a launcher icon — the ones in your app drawer. It is deliberately not QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES: apps without a launcher icon stay invisible, and the list is read on screen and never stored or sent.
List your apps on the Apps screen, so you can allow or mute each one\'s notifications
Look up an app\'s icon to colour the island from it
Check whether Shizuku is installed, to tell \"not installed\" apart from \"not running\"
